1:
Henry reads the passage first as a conditional promise belonging to all people and not to Israel only, and traces the repentance it requires through its stages. It begins in serious consideration, calling to mind what had been forgotten, since consideration is the first step towards conversion and the prodigal came to himself before he came to his father; and what is to be called to mind is precisely the blessing and the curse, as the prodigal weighed his present poverty against the plenty of bread in his father's house. Calvin limits the offer rather than the terms: God never so afflicts his Church as to be unready to return to mercy, but reconciliation is not held out indiscriminately, belonging by peculiar privilege to the Church and within it to the remnant, since it profits hypocrites mixed among believers no more than strangers to be scourged. Keil and Delitzsch explain why a blessing is named at all in a survey of coming judgment, since even in the deepest apostasy there would always be a holy seed which could not die out, the nation being otherwise utterly rejected and the promises brought to nothing.

Whether the gathering promised here has already happened divides the chapter's readers sharply. Clarke argues twice that it has not, since a dispersion among all nations must refer to a wider captivity than the Babylonian, and the repossession of the land must therefore be something other than the return from Chaldea. Gill goes further and treats a future restoration to Judea as the plain sense of many passages, adding that some of the dispersed are in this remote island of ours, once reckoned the uttermost part of the earth, and that others were firmly believed by Manasseh Ben Israel to be in America. Ellicott occupies the middle, holding it very difficult to interpret the words of any land but Palestine while pointing to Jeremiah for their fulfilment in the first restoration, and observing elsewhere that since the curse is still upon them the chapter contemplates a restoration still to come. Keil and Delitzsch deny both halves of the popular reading outright, holding that the promise neither points directly to a gathering of Israel on its ultimate conversion to Christ nor furnishes any proof that the Jews will then be brought back to Palestine.

Ellicott notices that the verb for turning the captivity is not active in the Hebrew as one would expect but neuter, and reports the inference the rabbis built on it: that the Shechinah abides with Israel through the stress of their captivity, so that God has prescribed redemption for himself and will return with them, and that the day of the gathering is so great and difficult that he must be there to take each man visibly by the hand. Ellicott then undercuts the inference himself by noting that the same form is used of Moab in Jeremiah, and lets the observation stand only as evidence of what the Jews expect. Calvin fixes on a smaller repetition, that the phrase from thence occurs twice so that distance should not be imagined an impediment to what God has promised, however unknown the country of their dispersion. Gill gives the Targum's paraphrase, that the Word of the Lord shall receive their repentance with good will, and Ellicott adds that the Greek version's wording for the outmost parts of heaven is traceable in the Gospel phrase about gathering from one end of heaven to the other.
6:
The circumcision of the heart is taken by all of them as the centre of the passage, and by Calvin as surpassing every other promise in it. He refers it to the new covenant, citing the passage in Jeremiah where God undertakes to put his law in their inward parts and write it in their hearts, and reads the metaphor from the legal sign of consecration: God will create them spiritually new men, cleansed from the filth of flesh and world and separated from the unclean nations. He then turns the verse into a lesson about sacraments, that circumcision was the sacrament of repentance as baptism now is, and that the letter is useless in itself, many being baptized to no profit, so that whatever God offers in a sacrament depends on the secret operation of his Spirit. Gill traces the same work through its stages in the converted Jew, the heart pricked and cut, the iniquity laid open, the hardness removed, the willingness to part with sin and with one's own righteousness, and observes that no circumcision of the flesh is mentioned here because that will be out of use once the ceremonial law is known to be abrogated.

Clarke draws a conclusion from the same verse that runs against the expectation of a national restoration. The heart of that people has never yet been circumcised and the promises of this chapter have never yet been fulfilled; but the law properly speaking made no provision for a circumcision of the heart, which implies remission of sins and purification of the soul, and circumcision itself was only the sign of a spiritual good. The promise therefore belongs to the days of the Messiah, and cannot be fulfilled to the Jews except in their embracing the gospel — from which he concludes that to look for their restoration while obstinacy and unbelief remain is idle and nugatory. Wesley reaches a similar destination by the order of events rather than by argument, that God will first convert and sanctify them, the fruit of which will be that they return and obey, and only then that they prosper; and he too refers the promise principally to the times of the gospel. Ellicott adds a separate reason for expecting something still to come, that the laws of this book have demonstrably never been kept perfectly, the Talmudic system having taken the heart out of them.

Two grammatical notes bear on how much is being promised and how much required. Keil and Delitzsch take the verb rendered thou shalt return as adverbial rather than a second command, meaning that Israel would hearken again, and prove it from the parallel in the following verse, where the Lord will return and rejoice plainly means will rejoice again. Ellicott makes the same kind of correction to the condition at the close, that the opening word rendered if comes from the Greek version while the Hebrew signifies for or when; Gill prefers the same reading, since it has already been promised that God would circumcise their hearts and that they should obey. Calvin and Wesley both resist letting the promise swallow the duty. Calvin observes that Moses requires here the perseverance he had just declared to be God's gift alone, and infers that they deal foolishly who estimate the powers of man by the commands of God, true conversion being proved by the constant tenor of the life. Wesley adds a count worth having: in the threatenings of the previous chapter God is called simply the Lord, but in these ten verses of promise he is called the Lord thy God twelve times.
11:
What the commandment is divides them before anything else. Gill notes that the Jews understand it of the law but holds that the apostle has taught us to read it of the word of faith, the gospel preached, which suits the context and the prophecies of conversion just delivered; Clarke likewise makes it the doctrine of salvation to be proclaimed in their own land, since the one who is to feed and save Israel is to be born at Bethlehem and the prophet who teaches them raised up from among their brethren. Keil and Delitzsch keep it firmly on the law, taking the phrase as it is used earlier in the book to denote the whole of it. Wesley threads between the two, taking it for the great command of loving and obeying God, the sum of the law, but not as it stands in itself, rather as softened and accompanied with the grace of the gospel: the practice of God's laws is in itself far from us and above our strength, yet with that grace it becomes near and easy to those who believe, which is how he squares the verse with the apostle's use of it for the righteousness of faith.

The two impossibilities the passage denies are read as answers to two real excuses. Henry sets them out plainly: no messengers need be sent to heaven to enquire what will please God, and no voyage need be made overseas as the philosophers made, travelling through many and distant regions in pursuit of learning, so that the command is within reach of men without estate or refined genius. Clarke and Wesley both keep the second image, Clarke observing shortly that salvation is of the Jews so they need not travel to distant nations for it, Wesley that the knowledge was brought to their very doors and declared to them in the wilderness. Gill turns it forward instead, that the gospel is ordered to be preached in all the world so that at the conversion of the Jews the earth will be filled with the knowledge of it as the waters cover the sea, and none will need to go into distant countries. Keil and Delitzsch state the same denials in the flattest terms, that the law was neither at an inaccessible height nor at an unattainable distance at the end of the world, so that no one could ask who is able to fetch it.

Calvin makes the verse a statement about the clarity of scripture and then a weapon. God does not propound obscure enigmas to keep our minds in suspense and torment us with difficulties, but teaches familiarly whatever is necessary, according to the capacity and therefore the ignorance of the people; nothing is required but diligent application, so that every pretext for ignorance is taken away and men cannot err except by wilfully shutting their eyes. From this he turns on those who hold scripture to be beset with thick darkness and drive the people away from it as from a labyrinth, saying they must either accuse the Holy Spirit of falsehood or malign the book itself; and he adds that if the ancient people were left without excuse, our stupidity deserves double and triple condemnation. On the last clause the three parts are distinguished. Henry has it in the mouth as being in the common tongue, spoken of familiarly among the children, and in the heart as being level to the meanest capacity. Clarke assigns the mouth to the promises forming part of every Jew's creed and the heart to the power of believing unto righteousness; Wesley sums it that the law is plain, and the gospel much more so.
15:
Henry reads the closing appeal as a piece of deliberate rhetoric and admires its construction. The manner of treating with them is so rational, so prudent and so affectionate that it shows the speaker in earnest and leaves them inexcusable; and it works on the two things by which every man is moved. Every man covets life and good and dreads death and evil, and here is the way to obtain the one and avoid the other; every man is governed by hope and fear, and both have now been tried, so that whoever will be wrought upon either way is kept close to his duty and whoever will not is without excuse. He adds a stroke of his own on the knowledge of good and evil: our first parents ate the forbidden fruit hoping to gain it, and got a miserable knowledge, of good by the loss of it and of evil by the sense of it, whereas God has since favoured man with such a knowledge of good and evil by his word as will make him happy for ever if it be not his own fault. Gill notes the speaker has returned to pressing the present observance of what he has delivered.

Clarke takes the setting of the two before them as a proof about the will, and states the case at length. He asks why they were set before them at all, and answers in four steps: that they might comprehend their import, that they might feel their importance, that they might choose the path of believing and loving obedience, and that in choosing they and their posterity might be God's favourites in time and eternity. Were there no such thing as free will in man, he asks, who could reconcile these sayings with either sincerity or common sense? He holds that God made the human will free in creation and formed the soul accordingly, that no power in heaven, earth or hell except God's own can deprive it of its free volitions, and that law and gospel, promise and precept, the denunciation of woe and the doctrine of eternal life are all constructed on that ground. From this he derives accountability: a man's actions are his and therefore rewardable and punishable, whereas actions necessitated by fate or sovereign constraint would not be his at all; and he adds that the principle of liberty is implied in the very idea of volition, so that a will not free would not be will.

Calvin arrives at the same verse by a different road and gives it a different weight. The point of setting the two before them is that Israel had no pretext of error, being separated from the heathen nations who vacillated as in uncertainty between life and death through ignorance of the right way; and since no one under the guidance of nature would fail to seek life and recoil from death, they are reproached as more than senseless if they plunge voluntarily into misery. He is careful that this should not sound like an idle menace, insisting the doctrine is armed with the power of God, so that whoever embraces it finds salvation and none despises it with impunity; and he takes the promises and threats together as what he calls the sanctions of the law, since its authority is only assured to us when both the recompense of obedience and the punishment of transgression are set before us. On the clause about being drawn away he refuses the mitigation it seems to offer, holding that it is named not to excuse their instability but to aggravate the crime, since they are carried off as by a whirlpool by their own depraved desires and desert a truth they knew well.
19:
On the summoning of heaven and earth, Gill offers two readings and Calvin rejects one of them. Gill will take it either literally, of the heavens above the speaker and the earth on which he stood, inanimate bodies frequently called upon as witnesses in matters of moment, or figuratively of the inhabitants of both, angels and men. Calvin says flatly that the words do not address men and angels, as some tamely expound them, but attribute sense to things inanimate by way of amplification; and he notes that although the verb stands in the past tense it indicates a present act, the witnesses being called in order to deal with the hearers more urgently. Keil and Delitzsch settle the grammar of the next clause instead, taking the words about choosing as the apodosis of the sentence, so that the calling of the witnesses is the protasis and the choice is what it drives at. Wesley reduces the whole to its bare consequence, that those shall have life who choose it, that whoever comes short of it must thank himself, and that they die because they will die.

The command to choose creates a difficulty Calvin states against himself before answering. As respects its doctrine the law contains life and death, since the reward of eternal life is not promised in it in vain; but because no one is found worthy of that reward, the apostle justly teaches that the law ministers death, which is accidental and proceeds from the corruption of men rather than any fault in the doctrine. How then, if our corruption makes the law engender nothing but death, can Moses command us to choose a life the sinner cannot reach by it? He notes that his opponents lift their crests at exactly this point, to extol free will and boast of merits, and answers that Moses also testifies the gratuitous mercy of God and directs his disciples to Christ, so that when he speaks of keeping the commandments he does not exclude the twofold grace, by which believers regenerated by the Spirit aspire to the obedience of righteousness while being freely reconciled through the pardon of their sins. Since the same covenant is common to us and the ancient people, he concludes that those who of old embraced this doctrine did in fact choose life.

Clarke takes the three verbs of the last verse as a chain in which no link will hold alone. Without love there can be no obedience; without obedience love is fruitless and dead; and without close attachment and perseverance, temporary love however sincere and fervent, and temporary obedience however disinterested and pure while it lasts, will be ultimately ineffectual, since he alone who endures to the end shall be saved. He then turns on a particular kind of confidence, observing that those who talk most strenuously about the impossibility of falling from grace are commonly those who have not yet tasted that the Lord is gracious, and asking how absurd it is to dispute about arriving safely at the end of a way in which a man has never taken one hearty step. Wesley expounds the clause that God is their life by accumulation, since he gives life, preserves it, restores it and prolongs it by his power though it be frail and by his presence though it be forfeited, sweetens it by his comforts and completes all in life everlasting. Ellicott hears in the same clause the Old Testament form of the saying about the resurrection and the life.
